title: The CEOs Who Held On Too Long
text:
Ulrike Malmendier and Geoffrey Tate wanted to find a way to measure overconfidence in real corporate leaders. Their idea was to look at what chief executives did with their own money. They studied CEOs of large American companies from 1980 to 1994.

Top executives are usually heavily exposed to their own firm already, through salary, bonuses and stock. A sensible executive should therefore exercise stock options once they are well in the money, to diversify. Yet some CEOs kept holding options until the year they expired, even when they could have locked in large gains. Malmendier and Tate argued that this behavior reflected a persistent belief that their company's stock would keep rising, in other words overconfidence in their own leadership.

These overconfident CEOs behaved differently with company money too. Their investment depended much more on how much cash the firm had on hand. When cash was plentiful, they invested heavily, apparently because they believed outside investors undervalued their firm and so they disliked raising new money. The effect was strongest in companies that relied on outside financing.
lesson: Leaders who believe too strongly in their own judgment overinvest when money is easy. Build in checks that test your plans against outside views.
source: Malmendier, U., and Tate, G. (2005). CEO overconfidence and corporate investment. Journal of Finance, 60(6), 2661-2700.
